questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
During my bachelor's I had taken a 2-year minor (sidefagspakke) in Japanese studies, but had been prevented from doing my exchange trip then, due to Covid.
So Japan was a natural choice for my semester abroad now. I applied to University of Tokyo partly because of its academic reputation, but mostly because of its cultural history, which stretches back to the late 19th century, and the modernization of Japan during the Meiji period. At this time, the great author Natsume Sōseki, in whose oeuvre I am interested academically, taught here for a while.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy. The only real hurdle was the registration at the city ward office, and the issuance of my national health insurance card – very few people in the administration speak english. But all went well, only patience is required, really.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: At the dormitory there was a very helpful help desk, and I went through an informative orientation at the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It would have been nice to have a student tutor to show around and give information about the facilities, extracurricular activities etc., but apart from that everything was good!

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was offered by the university – the application process was relatively simple, and the place was not too too expensive.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Choose the correct dorm to ease your commute! I took the train only for a couple of stops – no more than 30 mins of walking and train riding to get to uni. But Tokyo is a big place, and other dorms were placed much further from the primary campus. See if you can get information about what will be your primary campus before getting a place to stay.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I lived at the dorm in mejirodai (目白台). It was very big and kind of soulless – and there was really only a community among the exchange students, not at all like at danish dorms, where you hang out in the kitchens. But it was clean, conveniently located, and the facilities were great.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Only really complicated when taking courses from other graduate schools etc. – but all was in order in the end.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You only finalised the registration a couple of weeks into the semester – until then you could "shop around" and try dfferent things. A bit confusing, with having to find info through the various IT systems, but great that you can wait and see how the class feels before committing.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I got the help I needed from the support team at my graduate school, as well as from my academic advisor/host.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the classes I wanted, with no problems.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Shop around and try different courses in the first week – keep an open mind, and you'll definitely end up having fun and learning a lot.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: There was a lot of reading, and more (but smaller) exams than I'm used to – partly because I took two extra courses, because of some rule that said I had to have 10 hours of weekly classes. All of my courses were dicussion-based MA courses, so you really had to read for every week, but the material was pretty interesting, and the discussions were not too difficult to participate in.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Again, all of my classes were discussion-based, and had you do multiple student presentations etc. as well – I didn't find a single lecture class for MA level. But the kinds of critical discussions of texts were similar to what I am used to from seminars at the faculty of humanities at home, so there were no great difficulties.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
"Explaining" japanese religion: a critical approach
Gender and sexuality in japanese arts and culture
Historical perceptions in Asia – exploring various memories of world war 2
Visual culture, technology, and the everyday life
Law and the formation of transnational East Asia
The future of writing

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All of the above. The courses at my graduate school – Interdisciplinary Information Studies – can all be recommended, I feel like. And see if you can find a class on some kind of East Asian history taught by Matsubara at the faculty of Law, he's great!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Bank transfer fees, but they are not THAT overwhelming.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: You can eat pretty well for not a lot of money. Most things are less expensive than at home. And the national health insurance is a pretty good investment (and also mandatory...).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They were a bit difficult to find – especially as an MA student, I think. Many clubs were closed to exchange students who were only there for a semester. But the school festival was great, and the sports facilities at campus were pretty exceptional as well, and pretty cheap. Also, a language exchange program was offered, but I didn't have time to participate.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Go exploring in Tokyo, it is an amazing city! So many good, cheap places to eat (and drink!), nice museums, whole district of antiquarian bookshops, festivals (matsuri – you should definitely go to some, not least the fireworks ones!), very good thrift shops, etc.
And take some trips to the mountains, as well – there are great places to go hiking.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Again, go to the mountains. For example to Hakone, which really isn't too far away.
Also, you can take the bullet train (or the cheaper night bus) and get to pretty much anywhere on the main island pretty fast – at least a weekend's stay in Osaka or Kyoto is definitely recommended, or go during Golden week!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
Some people were a bit difficult to approach – there are definitely cultural differences in how we communicate and form relations. And many japanese are not very good at spoken english, which they are very shy about speaking. But most people are kind and really want to help etc.
Though my experience was that I quickly formed a bubble of other european exchange students...

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
If you live in a dorm, really do try to speak to people coming and going, cooking in th kitchen etc. – some of them really want to communicate, but most are very shy.
And feel free to e.g. organize a night out – your co-habitants will most likely be impressed by your initiative.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There is definitely a language barrier, and even though I speak a bit of japanese, communication with some was difficult.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Kind people, good food, amazing cultural sites (museums, temples and shrines(!!!), theatres), beautiful nature, etc.., and most everywhere feels very safe.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
You'll need to go through a lot of paperwork – but don't stress about it, everything always goes fine in the end, in my experience. And have patience with the IT systems as well. But do try to be on time when handing in papers, paperwork, coming to class, etc.. The japanese are punctual and appreciate that in other people.

Show up to a lot of courses during the first week, and try to feel out the vibe there, before committing.

And try to find time to go on a couple of trips. Skip a class or two, if need be, but remember: most classes have mandatory presence, so use your skips wisely, not just on sleeping in! And don't use too many saturdays at the library.. Get out and go to a festival – there's bound to be one going on somewhere in Tokyo!

Enjoy your trip. <3

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
You will receive your transcript (required for the credit transfer etc.) veeery late. But it will arrive eventually, though you might need to stall the SU people...

And remember: the trains in Japan only run until midnight!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I can't choose, but just being there, and having to figure out what to do on a sunday – and then going to some temple with friends I only just made – was amazing.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being very far from home, and in a +8 hour time zone sometimes made me feel very disconnected from everyone at home.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
